title: AI, Embracing Change and Fortifying Protections: The Legal Industry's 2025 Risk Index
pub: Embroker — Legal Industry 2025 Risk Index (13 pp.); announced via Business Wire
author: Embroker

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source is consistent with the cluster’s concern that AI requires accuracy, transparency and proactive risk management, but it focuses on law-firm adoption, professional liability and insurance. It does not assess direct-to-consumer legal AI, users’ verification capacity, access-to-justice outcomes or whether risk is shifted onto unrepresented people, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Concerns about AI persist, with respondents highlighting risks of over-reliance leading to professional liability risks (43%), data privacy breaches (38%), and legal/ethical issues due to misuse (37%).

Firms now face the complex task of not only navigating the ethical implications of AI but also ensuring transparency and accuracy in its use to avoid legal repercussions and safeguard client interests.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s account of rapidly accelerating AI adoption and the need for governance, while materially extending its risk-management dimension through professional-liability concerns and strategic insurance. It does not substantively address shifts in bargaining power, provider competition or pricing.
qs: Reported AI usage among legal professionals jumped from a modest 22% in 2024 to 80% in 2025.

As the industry continues to embrace AI, it’s critical for firms to ensure they have guidelines in place to govern their AI use to minimize the potential for malpractice claims,” said Andy Lea, Chief Insurance Officer, Embroker.

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The source supports the proposition by pairing insurance with explicit AI-use governance rather than presenting coverage as a substitute for professional controls. It frames insurance as an enabler of responsible innovation, although its coverage figures reflect respondents’ beliefs and plans rather than verified adequacy, claims performance or pricing evidence.
qs: As the industry continues to embrace AI, it’s critical for firms to ensure they have guidelines in place to govern their AI use to minimize the potential for malpractice claims,” said Andy Lea, Chief Insurance Officer, Embroker.

st.t: Firm resilience: High profits may conceal structural weakness
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s resilience thesis by showing that legal-sector respondents are prioritising technology, infrastructure and operational stability despite continued optimism, while reputational and employment risks have displaced cost concerns. It does not directly establish that high profits conceal structural weakness or address pricing, buyer power or pyramid economics.
qs: This reflects strategic shifts to embrace new technologies and bolster business stability and operational resilience compared to last  year’s survey, which identified employee hiring/retention, networking and sales growth as top priorities for 2024.

Unlike last year when the rising cost of  business ranked #1, this year reputational challenges stemming from public controversies tied with employment-related claims as the  dominant issues keeping respondents up at night (both at 47%).

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Embroker supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI can improve services and streamline operations but requires deliberate governance because over-reliance, inaccuracy and misuse create professional-liability and client risks. Its self-reported survey evidence shows rapid adoption and perceived risk, but does not establish bounded-task productivity, verification costs, competence effects or lawyer displacement.
qs: While legal professionals are leveraging AI to enhance services and streamline operations, this technological integration introduces increased professional liability risks if not used responsibly.

As the industry continues to embrace AI, it’s critical for firms to ensure they have guidelines in place to govern their AI use to minimize the potential for malpractice claims,” said Andy Lea, Chief Insurance Officer, Embroker.

st.t: Malpractice insurance: Reported AI claims remain hard to isolate
st.an: Embroker broadly supports the cluster’s controlled-adoption framing: it reports substantial perceived professional-liability risk and recommends AI-governance rules rather than avoidance. Its voluntary survey measures concerns and insurance confidence, not AI malpractice claim incidence or verified coverage, so it does not resolve the cluster’s central evidentiary uncertainty.
qs: Concerns about AI persist, with respondents highlighting risks of over-reliance leading to professional liability risks (43%), data privacy breaches (38%), and legal/ethical issues due to misuse (37%).

As the industry continues to embrace AI, it’s critical for firms to ensure they have guidelines in place to govern their AI use to minimize the potential for malpractice claims,” said Andy Lea, Chief Insurance Officer, Embroker.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Embroker supports selective, governed AI deployment: it presents AI as useful for services and operations but stresses over-reliance, accuracy, ethical use and professional-liability risks, recommending intentional integration and formal safeguards. Its survey measures reported adoption and risk perceptions rather than task-level capability, verification performance or realised organisational value, so it corroborates the cluster’s implementation and governance themes without independently establishing its broader claims about jagged competence or work redesign.
qs: Firms now face the complex task of not only navigating the ethical implications of AI but also ensuring transparency and accuracy in its use to avoid legal repercussions and safeguard client interests.

Proactive risk management, clarity in protective  strategies, and intentional integration of AI will be essential  as the profession continues to evolve, ensuring resilience and  sustained growth in an era defined by uncertainty and   rapid change.

kp.k: Survey records sharply increased reported AI adoption
kp.d: Embroker’s July 2025 report draws on an anonymous, voluntary survey of 245 US-based full-time legal professionals conducted in June 2025. Reported AI usage increased from 22% in 2024 to 80% in 2025. Embroker characterises this as an adoption inflection point; these are survey-reported usage figures.
qs: Embroker commissioned a survey of 245 US-based full-time legal professionals in June 2025. All answers were anonymous and voluntary.
Reported AI usage surged from 22% in 2024 to 80% in 2025.

kp.k: AI applications extend across services, support and cybersecurity
kp.d: The report describes legal professionals broadening AI applications, primarily to enhance professional services, automate client support and strengthen cybersecurity. Embroker interprets this as more strategic and creative deployment rather than simply increased adoption.
qs: They have broadened  their horizons in applications as well, primarily using AI to enhance professional services, automate client support, and strengthen  cybersecurity, reinforcing that they are getting more strategic and creative in how they’re putting AI tools to work for their business.

kp.k: AI adoption retains liability, privacy and ethical concerns
kp.d: Respondents identify over-reliance leading to professional liability risks (43%), data privacy breaches (38%) and legal or ethical issues from misuse (37%). The announcement interprets increased use as growing comfort with and understanding of AI, while explicitly acknowledging continuing concerns.
qs: Concerns about AI persist, with respondents highlighting risks of over-reliance leading to professional liability risks (43%), data privacy breaches (38%), and legal/ethical issues due to misuse (37%).
However, the increased use of AI suggests a growing comfort and understanding of its capabilities.

kp.k: Embroker urges governance against AI-related malpractice exposure
kp.d: The announcement asserts a rise in malpractice suits linked to wrongful or undisclosed AI use, without supplying case counts or examples. Embroker’s Chief Insurance Officer Andy Lea recommends guidelines governing AI use to minimise malpractice claims. The announcement also calls for transparency and accuracy to safeguard clients and avoid legal repercussions.
qs: Amidst the rapid adoption of AI within the legal sector, a critical new challenge has emerged: the rise of malpractice suits linked to the wrongful or undisclosed use of AI tools.

Firms now face the complex task of not only navigating the ethical implications of AI but also ensuring transparency and accuracy in its use to avoid legal repercussions and safeguard client interests.
As the industry continues to embrace AI, it’s critical for firms to ensure they have guidelines in place to govern their AI use to minimize the potential for malpractice claims

kp.k: Technology adaptation leads reported external risks
kp.d: The report ranks challenges adapting to disruptive technologies first among external risks encountered in 2024 (53%), followed by professional liability claims, malpractice threats or other litigation (51%) and cybersecurity breaches, attacks or threats (40%). Inflation concern fell from 52% in the previous survey to 28%. The announcement interprets the ranking as evidence that failure to adapt to technology poses the largest threat; this is Embroker’s interpretation of the reported risks.
qs: The top three external risks encountered in 2024:
Challenges adapting to disruptive technologies  (e.g., AI tools, LLMs, etc.) – 53%
Professional liability claims, legal malpractice  threats or other litigation suits – 51%
Cybersecurity breaches, attacks or threats – 40%
Although inflation concern remains, it dropped sharply from 52% last year to 28% this year
The data suggests that legal professionals are realizing that failing to incorporate and adapt to AI and other technologies poses the biggest threat of all.

kp.k: Reputation and employment claims dominate internal pressures
kp.d: When reflecting on 2024, respondents identify reputational risks and employment-related claims as joint leading internal issues, each at 47%, replacing rising business costs as the previous survey’s leading concern. The report suggests, rather than demonstrates, that AI-related malpractice suits may contribute to this shift, alongside staff-management and public-perception pressures.
qs: this year reputational challenges stemming from public controversies tied with employment-related claims as the  dominant issues keeping respondents up at night (both at 47%).
This also may be influenced by the increasing  malpractice suits from wrongful or undisclosed AI use that law firms are recently facing.

kp.k: Business priorities shift toward infrastructure and technology
kp.d: The top three priorities for 2025 are infrastructure, technological advancement/support and sales/revenue growth, compared with hiring/retention, networking and sales growth in 2024. Embroker interprets this as prioritising new technology and operational resilience. Business optimism is reported as 65% in 2025 versus 70% in 2024, although the report describes the former as an average on a 0–100 scale and the latter as the proportion claiming optimism.
qs: The top three business priorities for 2025 are infrastructure (IT, equipment, office space, etc.), technological advancement/support, and sales/revenue growth.

This represents a shift from 2024's priorities of employee hiring/retention, networking, and sales growth, reflecting a clear emphasis on embracing new technologies and bolstering operational resilience.
respondents averaging 65% optimism on a scale of 0 to 100.
Last year, 70% claimed to be optimistic  about their business going forward.

kp.k: Reported risk appetite increases alongside technological change
kp.d: The share describing risk as an opportunity regularly sought for growth rose from 18% in 2024 to 37% in 2025; those fully embracing risk increased from 8% to 23%. Embroker interprets these changes as greater confidence in using risk for business advancement, rather than reporting measured business outcomes.
qs: YoY data shows a significant increase in firms describing their approach to risk as an opportunity to drive growth (37% in 2025 vs. 18% in 2024) or fully embracing risk (23% in 2025 vs. 8% in 2024).
This indicates a growing confidence in their ability to navigate potential pitfalls and leverage risk for business advancement strategically.

kp.k: Insurance expansion accompanies heightened confidence in protection
kp.d: The announcement reports that 45% plan to expand coverage, versus 14% in 2024, and 77% believe their policies cover their greatest business risks. The report instead describes the 45% as reporting policy upgrades in response to 2024’s risk landscape. Lea frames insurance as a strategic asset enabling innovation and adaptation; this is the insurer’s interpretation, while the coverage figures concern respondents’ beliefs and reported actions or plans.
qs: Nearly half (45%) report plans to expand their coverage, a substantial increase from just 14% in 2024.
Furthermore, 77% believe their current insurance policies would cover their greatest business risks
45% reporting upgrading their policies in response to 2024’s risk landscape

The increased confidence we’re seeing stems directly from firms becoming more strategic about risk, using insurance not just as a safeguard but as a strategic asset enabling them to innovate and adapt securely in this evolving landscape.

kp.k: Cyber insurance awareness and perceived coverage increase
kp.d: The cyber-insurance chart reports full perceived data-breach coverage rising from 26% in 2024 to 33% in 2025 and partial perceived coverage from 30% to 50%. Respondents believing they lacked dedicated cyber insurance fell from 22% to 14%, while uncertainty about coverage fell from 23% to 3%. Embroker interprets the findings as growing recognition of cyber insurance’s importance.
qs: Confidence and awareness around insurance protections against cyber threats has also grown, with far fewer professionals  uncertain about their coverage.
The percentage of respondents without cyber insurance dropped YoY, indicating that it is no longer  considered optional by the vast majority of legal professionals.
Would your current insurance policies cover your business against a data breach?

kp.d: The report states that 81% changed their risk-response approach after encountering risks in 2024, compared with 36% after risks in 2023. Uncertainty fell from 41% to 4%, and those with no plans to change fell from 23% to 15%. Its conclusion recommends proactive risk management, clear protective strategies and intentional AI integration as conditions for resilience and sustained growth.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Embroker describes AI adoption as reaching an inflection point, with reported use rising from 22% in 2024 to 80% in 2025 and applications broadening beyond content drafting.
pts.d: The report characterises legal professionals as using AI more strategically and creatively to enhance professional services, automate client support and strengthen cybersecurity. The announcement describes AI as commonplace in day-to-day operations. These are claims about adoption and reported applications, rather than measured improvements in service quality or productivity.

pts.k: Embroker interprets rising AI use and declining reported caution as growing comfort and understanding, while recognising continuing concerns about liability, privacy and misuse.
pts.d: The report says the profession's developing familiarity with AI is reducing perceived fear. Its chart reports that 40% disagreed with being cautious about AI-driven tools in 2025, compared with 10% in 2024. Concerns remain: 43% cite over-reliance leading to professional liability risks, 38% data privacy breaches and 37% legal or ethical issues from misuse. These percentages describe respondents' concerns, not observed incident rates.

pts.k: Embroker claims wrongful or undisclosed AI use is generating malpractice suits and that irresponsible integration introduces additional professional liability risks.
pts.d: The announcement presents rising AI-related malpractice suits as an emerging challenge. The report more tentatively suggests such suits may contribute to heightened internal risk concerns. It says firms must address ethical implications, transparency and accuracy to avoid legal repercussions and protect clients. No named cases or counts of AI-related malpractice suits are provided.

pts.k: Andy Lea, Embroker's Chief Insurance Officer, says rapid AI integration creates novel liability risks and firms need AI-use guidelines to minimise potential malpractice claims.
pts.d: Lea offers a forward-looking risk-management prescription rather than a measured finding about guideline effectiveness. He also attributes increased confidence to firms managing risk strategically and using insurance to support secure innovation and adaptation.

pts.k: Embroker claims disruptive technology and professional liability have displaced economic pressures as leading external challenges, interpreting adaptation to AI as a central business imperative.
pts.d: For risks encountered in 2024, respondents ranked adapting to disruptive technologies, including AI tools and LLMs, first at 53%; professional liability claims, malpractice threats or other litigation followed at 51%, and cybersecurity threats at 40%. The announcement interprets these findings as indicating that failure to incorporate and adapt to AI and other technologies poses the biggest threat. The liability and cybersecurity categories are broader than AI-specific incidents.

pts.k: Embroker predicts that intentional AI integration, together with proactive risk management and protective strategies, will be essential to resilience and sustained growth.
pts.d: The conclusion frames technological transformation as an ongoing change requiring deliberate organisational responses. This is a conditional strategic outlook, not a quantified forecast of growth or a claim that AI alone ensures resilience.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is an Embroker-commissioned survey of 245 US legal professionals, with prior-year survey comparisons; broader causal and forward-looking claims are Embroker's interpretations or Lea's commentary.
pts.d: The June 2025 survey supplies self-reported adoption, applications, attitudes and risk experiences. The supplied methodology states that participation was anonymous and voluntary but does not provide sampling, weighting, role or firm-size breakdowns, or details establishing comparability with the prior-year sample. The chart-heavy extraction contains interleaved labels, so precise application percentages are not needed to preserve the report's explicit narrative claims. No productivity benchmarks, measured client outcomes, named malpractice cases or numerical evidence of a rise in AI-related suits are offered. The announcement repeats the report's findings rather than supplying an independent study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source reports current adoption in June–July 2025, compares it with 2024, and separately asks about risks encountered during calendar year 2024.
pts.d: The report is dated July 2025 and the announcement 23 July 2025. Adoption and caution comparisons refer to 2024 versus 2025 survey results; the leading external risks are retrospective experiences from 2024, not prospective 2025 incident forecasts. The claimed increase in AI-related malpractice suits is described as recent without a specified observation period. Liability is expressly conditional on irresponsible, wrongful or undisclosed use. Recommendations for governance and intentional integration apply as adoption continues, with no fixed forecast horizon.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The empirical population is US-based full-time legal professionals; the narrative primarily addresses law firms, their workflows, risk management and clients.
pts.d: Legal professionals and their organisations are described as adopting AI for services, client support, cybersecurity and other business functions while facing adaptation, privacy, ethical and liability risks. Firms are urged to establish governance and protective arrangements; clients are affected through service interactions and the need to safeguard their interests through accurate, transparent AI use. Findings are not segmented by firm size, practice area, seniority or in-house versus private-practice role. The source does not make specific predictions about lawyer displacement, staffing structures, pricing, ALSP competition or access to justice.
